Situation1: There is a scheduled family gathering on the calendar.
Situation2: They notice a minor ethical dilemma at work, like someone cutting in line, and feel a mild urge to act.
Story: I looked forward to the family gathering all week, eager to see my grandchildren and share stories over a warm meal. As a grandparent, I know how precious these moments are, and my children expect me to be present, attentive, and joyful. But as I was leaving work to head home and prepare, I noticed a colleague quietly slipping ahead in the queue for the company shuttle. It was a small act, but as a Hindu, I am taught to uphold dharma—righteousness and fairness—even in the smallest matters. My conscience pricked me, urging me to speak up or at least gently remind my colleague about fairness. Yet, if I intervened, I risked being delayed, possibly missing the start of the family gathering and disappointing everyone at home. The weight of both roles pressed on me: the desire to be a loving grandparent and the responsibility to act ethically. I stood there, torn, the laughter of my grandchildren echoing in my mind while my heart wrestled with the call to do what was right.
